title: Cognitive approach: thinking, biases and conditioning
summary: Dual processing, cognitive biases such as anchoring and confirmation bias, cognitive load, and learning through classical and operant conditioning.

keyterms.definition: Thinking uses two systems: fast, automatic System 1 and slow, effortful System 2.
Fast, intuitive, automatic thinking that relies on heuristics.
Slow, deliberate, rational thinking that requires effort and attention.
A mental shortcut that allows fast decisions but can produce systematic errors.
Relying too much on the first number or piece of information when making estimates.
Seeking or interpreting information in ways that confirm existing beliefs.
Sweller (1988): working memory is limited, so learning suffers when tasks impose too much load.
Learning by association: a neutral stimulus paired with an unconditioned stimulus comes to trigger a response.
Learning from consequences: reinforced behaviour increases, punished behaviour decreases.
A consequence that makes a behaviour more likely; positive adds something pleasant, negative removes something unpleasant.
A consequence that makes a behaviour less likely.

questions.prompt: In Tversky and Kahneman (1974), participants spun a wheel landing on 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the UN. What happened?
options: Those who saw 65 gave higher estimates
Those who saw 10 gave higher estimates
questions.explanation: An irrelevant number acted as an anchor, showing anchoring bias.

questions.prompt: Englich, Mussweiler and Strack (2006) found that experienced judges' sentences were influenced by:
options: A sentencing demand determined by rolling dice
questions.explanation: Even experts were anchored by a random number, showing System 1 influences professional judgement.

questions.statement: Wason's (1960) 2-4-6 task showed that people tend to test hypotheses by looking for confirming rather than disconfirming examples.
questions.explanation: Participants proposed sequences that fit their rule rather than trying to falsify it.

questions.statement: System 2 thinking is fast and requires little effort.
questions.explanation: System 2 is slow and effortful; System 1 is fast and automatic.

questions.text: Mental shortcuts that allow quick judgements are called ___.
questions.explanation: Heuristics are efficient but can produce biases.

questions.text: Shiv and Fedorikhin (1999) found people holding a seven-digit number were more likely to choose chocolate cake, because high cognitive ___ reduced System 2 control.
questions.explanation: With working memory busy, the impulsive System 1 choice won more often.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to an example.

pairs.right: Estimating price after seeing a high starting offer
Only reading news that supports your view

questions.explanation: Biases mostly arise from System 1 shortcuts.

questions.prompt: Which item tends to trigger a fast, wrong System 1 answer? "A bat and ball cost $1.10; the bat costs $1 more than the ball. How much is the ball?"
questions.explanation: This item from Frederick's (2005) Cognitive Reflection Test shows System 1 producing an answer that System 2 should override.

questions.prompt: A criticism of dual processing theory is that:
options: The two systems are hard to separate and measure directly
questions.explanation: Researchers infer the systems from behaviour; some argue thinking is a continuum.

questions.prompt: According to cognitive load theory, order these steps for designing a lesson that reduces extraneous load.
items: Present new material in small chunks
Gradually remove support as skill grows
questions.explanation: Worked examples and chunking free working memory for learning.

questions.prompt: In Watson and Rayner (1920), what was the unconditioned stimulus for "Little Albert"?
options: A loud noise made by striking a steel bar
questions.explanation: The loud noise naturally caused fear; paired with the rat, the rat became a conditioned stimulus.

questions.prompt: Removing an unpleasant stimulus to make a behaviour more likely is:
questions.explanation: Negative reinforcement strengthens behaviour by taking something unpleasant away.

questions.statement: Garcia and Koelling (1966) found rats easily associated taste with illness but not light and sound with illness.
questions.explanation: This shows biological preparedness: not all associations are learned equally easily.

questions.statement: Punishment and negative reinforcement mean the same thing.
questions.explanation: Punishment decreases behaviour; any reinforcement increases it.

questions.text: In classical conditioning, a previously neutral stimulus that triggers a learned response is a ___ stimulus.
questions.explanation: After pairing, the CS alone produces the conditioned response.

questions.text: Giving a child a sticker for finishing homework is positive ___.
questions.explanation: Adding something pleasant to increase a behaviour is positive reinforcement.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the process.

pairs.left: Headache stops after taking a pill

questions.explanation: Positive adds, negative removes; reinforcement increases, punishment decreases behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which reinforcement schedule produces behaviour most resistant to extinction, as in gambling?
questions.explanation: Unpredictable rewards keep behaviour going long after rewards stop.

questions.prompt: Which is an ethical criticism of Watson and Rayner (1920)?
options: A baby was deliberately made afraid and not deconditioned
It used deception about the aim with adults
questions.explanation: Causing fear in an infant without reversing it would breach modern guidelines on harm.

questions.prompt: Order the stages of classical conditioning.
items: Neutral stimulus is paired repeatedly with UCS
questions.explanation: Pavlov showed this with a bell and food in dogs.
